title: Waymo files two recalls over closed freeway lanes and police hand directions
excerpt: Waymo has told US safety regulators about two software recalls: one for cars that may drive into closed freeway lanes, one for responding to officers directing traffic.

sources.title: Claims Journal (Reuters): Waymo Recalls Self-Driving Cars Over Closed Freeway Lanes, Manual Traffic Control
Fox Business via Yahoo News: Waymo issues double safety recall days after California bans robotaxis from freeways

body_html:
Waymo, which runs driverless taxi services in several US cities, has filed two safety recalls with the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the federal agency responsible for vehicle safety. Waymo announced the recalls on Friday 20 November 2026 and said it had filed them the day before, according to Reuters and Fox Business.

Both recalls cover the software that drives the cars, which Waymo calls the Waymo Driver. In the United States, a "recall" is the formal process a maker uses to report a safety defect and fix it. For a driverless car, the fix is usually a software update sent over the air, and the cars do not have to go to a workshop.

What happened

According to both reports, which draw on Waymo's announcement:

  • Closed freeway lanes. In unusual circumstances, a Waymo car may enter a closed freeway lane and keep driving in it. Waymo said no collisions or injuries had been reported from these events. It said it is still working on the fix.
  • Directions from police and emergency staff. The second recall concerns how the cars respond when an officer or other emergency worker directs traffic by hand at an intersection. It followed a collision in which a Waymo car followed an officer's directions, but the officer then became temporarily blocked from the car's view. Waymo said the software update for this issue was completed on 6 November 2026.

In a statement quoted by Fox Business, Waymo said: "We hold our technology to high safety standards and take proactive actions whenever we see opportunities to improve performance." It described the recalls as standard steps in validating its technology as it moves into more complex driving environments.

The recalls come days after California's Department of Motor Vehicles barred Waymo's driverless cars from the state's freeways, citing repeated entries into active construction zones. Humasure News covered that decision on 19 November. Reuters reports that Waymo has halted freeway operations in the United States. Rides on ordinary city streets continue.

What is still unknown

  • How many vehicles each recall covers, and the recall numbers. Neither report gives them, and NHTSA's filings were not available to us at the time of writing.
  • When and where the collision involving police directions took place, and whether anyone was hurt.
  • When the fix for closed freeway lanes will be ready, and how its effectiveness will be checked before freeway service resumes.
  • Whether NHTSA will take any further step. Neither report includes a statement from the agency on these two recalls.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

Closed lanes and hand signals from police are exactly the kind of situation where a driverless car has to recognise that the normal rules have changed. Humasure's Directive 2, Bounded autonomy, asks that an automated system know the limits of the conditions it was designed for and act safely at the edge of them. Directive 3, Physical safety, covers the risk to road workers, police and other drivers when a vehicle ends up where it should not be.

Software recalls also touch Directive 10, Safe for its whole life: a vehicle's safety keeps changing as its software is updated, so each fix needs to be tested and reported. Directive 9, Accountable, is about someone answering for the system. A public recall filing is one way that happens.

Incidents like these are a reason for clear, independent standards, not a reason to fear the technology. Driverless cars are being tested in complex places, and public reporting of problems and fixes is part of how that work stays visible.

Questions you can ask any maker

  • How does the vehicle recognise a closed lane, a work zone or a person directing traffic, and what does it do when it is unsure?
  • Who decides when a software fix is ready, and how is it tested before it reaches the road?
  • Where can the public see recalls, incident reports and the results of fixes?

More questions are on our page of questions to ask before you trust an AI product or robot.
